lessons.title: pater, mater — the oldest words, kept close to the source
lessons.gloss: father and mother — the PIE ancestor Latin and English both inherited, in parallel

segments.text: "Father" and "mother" are among the oldest reconstructible words in human language. Latin kept them almost exactly as they were; English took the very same ancestor down a different road.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: Cousins, not parent and child

segments.text: Here's the point worth getting exactly right: pater and English father are not one derived from the other. Both descend independently, in parallel, from the same PIE word. Latin simply kept the ancestral p and t close to unchanged; the Germanic branch that produced English took a separate route through Grimm's Law, which shifted that same inherited p becomes f and t becomes th:

utterances: PIE ancestor: ph₂tḗr. Latin: pater. Germanic becomes English: father.
PIE ancestor: méh₂tēr. Latin: māter. Germanic becomes English: mother.

segments.text: So pater and father are siblings, sharing one parent-word thousands of years back — not a case of English borrowing or descending from Latin. Pater also gives Latin (and later English, through Latin) the whole "of-a-parent" family: paternus ("fatherly," becomes English paternal) and māternus ( becomes maternal).

segments.text: Does English father come from Latin pater? (No — both descend independently from the same PIE word, ph₂tḗr.) What sound-law explains the difference between them? (Grimm's Law — the Germanic branch shifted the inherited p becomes f, t becomes th; Latin kept them.) What Latin adjectives give English paternal and maternal? (Paternus, māternus.)

lessons.title: frater, soror — Latin's original siblings, before Spanish moved on
lessons.gloss: brother and sister — the words Vulgar Latin later abandoned in favor of germanus

segments.text: Two more ancient words — and a preview of a twist: these are the very words that later got pushed aside in everyday Latin, on the road to Spanish.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: Cousins with English, not ancestors of it

segments.text: Same rule as pater/māter: frāter is not the source of English "brother" — they're cousins, both from bʰréh₂tēr, with Grimm's Law shifting the Germanic branch's bʰ becomes b while Latin developed its own f (from an earlier bʰ becomes f shift already inside Latin itself).

Soror is the more surprising one. English sister looks nothing like soror — and that's because Latin dropped the w from the PIE cluster sw- (giving plain s-), while the Germanic branch kept the w far longer (Old English had sweostor). So soror and sister are, once again, cousins from the same PIE word, swésōr — neither one turned into the other; each branch just handled that opening sw- differently.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: Be honest about what happened next: germanus took over

segments.text: Here's the twist: classical Latin could say frāter germānus, "a brother of the same blood," to mark a full sibling. Over time, in everyday (Vulgar) Latin, that adjective germānus took over the whole job, and frāter itself faded out of common use — which is exactly why Spanish says hermano, not a descendant of frāter at all. (French frère took the opposite path and kept frāter as its everyday word — different Latin regions, different survivors.)

segments.text: Is English "sister" descended from Latin soror? (No — both are cousins from PIE swésōr; Latin dropped the w, Germanic kept it longer.) What Latin phrase eventually replaced frāter in everyday speech, and where does it show up today? (Frāter germānus becomes just germānus becomes Spanish hermano.) Did every Romance language make that same swap? (No — French kept frāter as frère; Spanish moved on to germānus.)
